papers.title: REPAIR: Resolving Long-Tail Confusion in Scientific Retrievers via Fact-Verified Iterative Refinement
papers.summary: Diagnoses long-tail concept failures in scientific retrievers, expands evidence through APIs, and iteratively repairs training data using fact verification and hard-negative mining. The method outperforms 19 baselines across nine benchmarks spanning materials science and biomedicine.
papers.use: This is directly relevant to drug-target-response and cell-cell communication RAG systems, where rare genes, drugs, and relation types are exactly where retrieval tends to break down. It provides a concrete way to repair that weakness during training.
papers.steal: Diagnose retrieval failures by concept-frequency bands and confusion pairs, then close the loop with evidence APIs, hard negatives, and retraining.
papers.doubt: Synthetic queries or API-derived evidence may teach benchmark-specific phrasing. I would want to test whether recall for unseen drug-target relations improves on a real PubMed corpus without increasing citation errors.

papers.title: Hyperbolic Graph Representation Learning for Differential Diagnosis on Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
papers.authors: Pietro Miotto, Lucia Mellini, Tommaso Marzi, Cesare Alippi, Elena Casiraghi, Alberto Paccanaro, Giorgio Valentini, Mauricio Soto-Gomez
papers.summary: Embeds a heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graph containing phenotypes, diseases, genes, proteins, and patients in hyperbolic space for Mendelian disease ranking. On ontology structure, hyperbolic embeddings are strong at lower dimension than Euclidean alternatives, and the paper also evaluates diagnostic link prediction on patient-integrated graphs.
papers.use: This maps well to a KG that must combine hierarchical ontologies with cross-cutting drug-target and cell-communication edges. It also gives a principled reason to choose the representation geometry rather than treating it as another generic GNN comparison.
papers.steal: Use hyperbolic geometry for ontology-derived tree structure, relation-aware scoring for cross-cutting edges, and evaluate representation efficiency separately by structural edge type.
papers.doubt: The study is preliminary, and it is unclear whether low-dimensional advantages translate into better final diagnosis or OOD patient performance. Euclidean baselines should be checked under matched parameter budgets and negative sampling.

papers.title: Evidence-Grounded Agentic Formulation Development in an Autonomous Laboratory
papers.authors: Michael M. Craig, Riley J. Hickman, Yingshan Ma, Rémi Piché-Taillefer, Christine Allen, Pauric Bannigan
papers.summary: Andromeda 2 is an agent that uses structured internal experimental evidence plus computational and wet-lab tools to design formulation batches sequentially. In a paclitaxel SEDDS setting, it reports a 50% high-performance hit rate, while an ablation removing evidence access reduces mean AUC by 34%.
papers.use: This is a concrete example of moving beyond prediction toward a scientific agent that chooses the next intervention using past experimental evidence. It could be a useful reference for connecting perturbation models such as PerturbRx to experimental decision-making.
papers.steal: Log the exact experimental records and tool outputs used for each agent decision, then ablate evidence access to quantify how much grounded evidence actually contributes.
papers.doubt: The evaluation is limited to one drug and one formulation system, and automation differences may be mixed with agent-design effects even under the same budget. Replication across drugs and laboratories is the key test.

papers.title: Time-Aligned Evolving Concept Graphs for Scientific Relation Forecasting
papers.authors: Fred Sun, Jingze Wang, Minkun Xu, Shangqi Guo
papers.summary: Treats each dated paper as a synchronized update event for both semantic and graph state, then predicts the emergence, formation, and type of concept relations using only information available up to the prediction time. Updating context improves mean relation AUPRC by 16.6% over frozen context.
papers.use: For a PubMed-backed evidence graph, this is a useful template for avoiding leakage of future knowledge into the present graph. It transfers naturally to temporal evaluation of novel drug-target hypotheses.
papers.steal: Use paper timestamps as the single clock for jointly updating text embeddings and graph edges, and construct time-sliced negatives for evaluation.
papers.doubt: Despite high AUROC, the population-weighted AUPRC is only 0.005778. The practical question is whether precision remains useful at realistic candidate counts and whether the model is doing more than frequency prediction.

papers.title: When Is Graph Structure Worth Its Cost? The Case for Structure Pricing in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Yuzhong Zhang, Haoyang Ma, Chao Peng, Lionel Briand, Boxi Yu, Jialun Cao
papers.summary: Evaluates GraphRAG not only on answer quality but also ingestion and query cost, and proposes EffiRAG, which uses graph structure primarily to locate source passages. On the 120-question UltraDomain benchmark, it is preferred over LightRAG-hybrid more often while reducing total cost by 57%.
papers.use: This is a good framework for preventing a biomedical KG/RAG project from treating graph construction as an end in itself. It asks when structural retrieval is actually worth its cost for a given query type.
papers.steal: Compare vector-only, graph-only, and hybrid retrieval on the same corpus along three axes: answer quality, evidence preservation, and ingestion/query cost.
papers.doubt: The benchmark is small at 120 questions across four domains, and judge robustness matters. The main test is whether the cost advantage survives multi-hop biomedical QA and frequently changing corpora.

papers.title: HPOQuest: A Rare-Disease Diagnostic Agent Using Active Phenotype Acquisition
papers.authors: Kamilia Zaripova, Nassir Navab, Azade Farshad, Annalisa Marsico
papers.summary: Maintains a disease posterior from a small set of observed phenotypes and actively selects which phenotype to ask about next. Across four cohorts, the training-free agent improves Recall@1 from sparse evidence by as much as 30 percentage points.
papers.use: The problem framing transfers well from diagnosis to experimental science: instead of passively embedding available observations, choose the next measurement that most reduces predictive uncertainty, such as an additional assay or perturbation.
papers.steal: Separate candidate ranking from data acquisition and use information gain to choose the next observation to collect.
papers.doubt: Improvements based on simulated answers may not survive real clinical missingness, recording errors, or acquisition costs. Overfitting to a fixed question set is another concern.

papers.title: Decoding Extrahepatic Targeting of Lipid Nanoparticles with Interpretable Machine Learning
papers.authors: Asal Mehradfar, Mohammad Shahab Sepehri, Owen Antholine, Varun Shankar, Glen S. Kwon, Salman Avestimehr, Morteza Rasoulianboroujeni
papers.summary: Integrates 476 lipid nanoparticle formulations from 81 studies and predicts extrahepatic accumulation from lipid structural descriptors and formulation ratios. XGBoost reaches ROC-AUC 0.874, while a consensus set of the top 20 features retains nearly all predictive information.
papers.use: This is a useful example of building a literature-derived drug-delivery dataset and combining molecular structure with formulation context. It could inform a pipeline that turns an evidence graph into a predictive table.
papers.steal: Aggregate SHAP rankings across multiple models and compress them into a small, reproducible set of design rules rather than relying on one model's explanation.
papers.doubt: Differences in measurement protocols across studies and within-study train/test leakage could inflate performance. A leave-one-study-out evaluation would be more convincing.

papers.title: Bad Genius: Counterfactual-Guided Harness Evolution Beyond Task-Specific Shortcuts
papers.authors: Guojun Zhu, Xunheng Huang, Peng Yin, Jiahui Xie, Sanguo Zhang, Doudou Zhou
papers.summary: Addresses the problem that optimizing an agent's prompt, memory, retrieval, and tools against one benchmark can reward protocol-specific shortcuts. CHASE introduces a Challenger that generates validity-preserving counterfactual protocols intended to expose and remove those shortcuts.
papers.use: Scientific agents and RAG pipelines can easily optimize benchmark-specific harness quirks rather than scientific capability. This provides a useful analogue of transfer-trust testing for agent systems.
papers.steal: Vary scoring order, tool surfaces, and presentation formats while preserving task meaning, then measure how much of the original performance gain is destroyed.
papers.doubt: The key question is whether automated counterfactuals truly preserve meaning. Human audits outside OfficeQA would help distinguish shortcut removal from simply making the task harder.

papers.title: Decodability is Not Causality: Dissociating Probe Readouts from Behavioral Drivers via SAE Decomposition
papers.authors: Devesh Tiwari, Camille Davis, Shivank Sinha, Talia Weaver, Aditya Shah, Maheep Chaudhary
papers.summary: Shows that a concept being decodable by a linear probe does not imply that the model actually uses those features to drive behavior. SAE features are ranked by probe alignment and behavioral gradient, and the overlap between the two rankings is only about 12%.
papers.use: The same warning applies to biological representations: being able to decode a cell state is not the same as showing that the predictive mechanism relies on that axis. This is a useful experimental template for avoiding causal overclaims from probes.
papers.steal: After demonstrating readout accuracy, add an activation-aware feature-selection step followed by intervention and behavioral change as a required causal check.
papers.doubt: The result is centered on one truth-probe setting and a narrow model family. SAE dictionary instability and off-manifold effects from ablation also need to be separated from true causal importance.

papers.title: Changepoint-Aware World Models: Detecting Dynamics Shifts and Recovering by Forgetting Stale Replay in Model-Based RL
papers.summary: Applies online CUSUM to DreamerV3 prediction error to detect abrupt dynamics shifts, then keeps the learned representation while discarding stale replay data. This speeds recovery after changes in gravity or actuator gain compared with passive retraining.
papers.use: The idea may transfer to biological settings where cell line, batch, or treatment regime changes make old data actively harmful. It suggests a way to manage continual updates to a world model without blindly mixing stale and current observations.
papers.steal: Warm-start the representation but reset only the data memory after a detected change, separating persistent knowledge from stale experience.
papers.doubt: The evidence focuses on abrupt simulated shifts and only a few seeds. Gradual drift and false positives may be much harder, especially when distinguishing a true regime change from noise.
